questions.q: State the three discussion prompts given in the "Talking about the Text" section of Forster's essay "The Story".
questions.a: The three prompts are: (1) "What does a novel do?" (2) "Our daily life reflects a double allegiance to 'the life in time' and 'the life by values'." (3) "The description of novels as organisms." A wrong answer that lists the "Appreciation" questions or "Understanding the Text" questions reveals the student has not distinguished between the different exercise sections in the textbook.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what Forster means by the "double allegiance" of daily life, using the example he gives ("I only saw her for five minutes, but it was worth it").
questions.a: Forster means that we live simultaneously in chronological time (the five minutes) and in value-intensity (the "worth it" moment). The first allegiance measures duration; the second measures significance. A wrong answer that only defines "life in time" as "schedule" and "life by values" as "morals" misses the temporal vs. intensity contrast central to Forster's argument.

questions.q: During a discussion on Prompt 1, a peer says: "Forster thinks novels are only good for entertainment because he calls the story 'the lowest and simplest of literary organisms'." Using a specific phrase from the essay, correct this misinterpretation.
questions.a: Forster immediately adds: "Yet it is the highest factor common to all the very complicated organisms known as novels." The student must quote "highest factor common to all" to show the story is necessary but not sufficient. A wrong answer that agrees with the peer reveals a failure to track Forster's concessive structure ("Yet...").

questions.q: Compare the "organism" metaphor in Prompt 3 with the "tape-worm" and "backbone" metaphors earlier in the essay. What does the shift from parasitic to organic imply about Forster's evolving view of the story?
questions.a: The tape-worm/backbone images suggest the story is a parasitic or skeletal necessity — something the novel must carry but not celebrate. The "organism" metaphor elevates the novel to a living, integrated whole where the story is one vital system among others. A wrong answer that treats all three metaphors as identical misses Forster's rhetorical progression from disdain to structural respect.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "Forster's three voices represent three types of readers, but the third voice (his own) is the only one a serious literature student should adopt." Defend or challenge using evidence from the essay.
questions.a: Challenge: Forster says he "respects and admires the first speaker" (the vague, good-tempered one) because that voice acknowledges the story's fundamentality without pretension. The third voice is his own regretful acceptance, not a prescription. A serious student should recognize all three as genuine readerly stances. A wrong answer that uncritically endorses the third voice shows inability to distinguish authorial persona from pedagogical recommendation.

questions.q: Create a 30-second opening statement for a discussion on Prompt 2 that hooks the group with a modern example (social media, gaming, etc.) and explicitly ties it to Forster's "life by values" phrase.
questions.a: "Think of a 15-second Reel that makes you cry — chronologically it's nothing, but in 'life by values' it's a pinnacle. Forster says daily life 'piles up into a few pinnacles' — that Reel is a pinnacle. Who else has a 'five minutes but worth it' moment from this week?" A poor answer that merely summarizes the prompt without a contemporary hook shows inability to bridge text and lived experience.
